sentences.text: The genus name Kairuku combines Māori words for food and diving.
The species name waewaeroa translates to long legs, describing the bird's elongated hind limbs.
K. grebneffi stood 1.28 meters tall, while K. waewaeroa could reach a height of 1.38 meters.
This species possesses the longest humerus bone of any penguin known from either the fossil record or living species.
It had a longer bill and a more slender body compared to living penguin species.
Relative to its body size, K. grebneffi had flippers that were longer and likely more flexible than those of extant penguin species.
Kairuku fossils date to 27 million years ago and were found in the Kokoamu Greensand Formation of New Zealand.
The first Kairuku bones were discovered in 1977 by Ewan Fordyce, though they were not identified as Kairuku at that time.
In February 2012, a team led by Fordyce and Daniel Ksepka reconstructed a K. grebneffi skeleton using specimens from the Kokoamu Greensand of New Zealand.
The holotype of K. grebneffi was collected in 1991 from the Waipati stream drainage area in New Zealand.
Fossils of K. waewaeroa, known as the Kawhia giant penguin, were found in Kawhia Harbour on New Zealand's North Island.
Predators of K. grebneffi likely included sharks and Squalodons.
Kairuku was historically classified under the genus Palaeeudyptes.
The genus Kairuku was described by Ksepka, Fordyce, Ando & Jones in 2012.
K. grebneffi lived in what is now New Zealand during the late Oligocene, roughly 25 to 27 million years ago.
During the late Oligocene, the area now known as New Zealand consisted mostly of ocean with a few isolated islands.
Researchers believe that rock outcrops provided safe breeding grounds and access to rich food resources for K. grebneffi.
